wa_alpenglow_aka_upper_kueffler_road_bou.blurb: A small boulder field on a hilltop clearing in the Columbia Gorge, up a gravel road from Beacon Rock. Twelve problems are logged, running from easy slabs through a broad middle of V0 to V2 and a handful of harder lines up to roughly V7. The largest block is about forty feet long and offers several lines, with slabs, steep traverses, roofs and dihedrals spread around the clearing. The rock is clean with very little lichen and high friction that can be hard on skin, and some landings are rough enough to want pads and a spotter. Being exposed to the sun for most of the day, the boulders dry quickly, though wind can be strong.

wa_bend_center.blurb: The tallest stretch of cliff at The Bend, above the Tieton River southwest of Yakima. All twelve routes are trad, mostly 5.9 and 5.10 with a single 5.12 at the top end. Climbs on the left start straight from the ground and run two pitches, while the ones on the right are long single pitches that begin from a prominent ledge system, reached by a short scramble. The Bend as a whole is known for finger and hand cracks, and it is popular with climbers working through the 5.10 trad grades.

wa_little_dishman.blurb: A small granite outcrop in Spokane, just east of the main Dishman wall. Short bolted lines dominate, with ten sport routes, one top-rope and one trad line. Grades run from about 5.6 to 5.11, with the bulk in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, which makes it a handy spot for climbers stepping up from the easier grades and for quick after-work laps close to town. The walk from the gate is brief, and a smaller cliff sits a short distance beyond.

wa_the_alcove.blurb: A bouldering pocket in the Barney's Rubble hollow of Icicle Creek, near Leavenworth, around 1,700 feet up. It tucks in behind a couple of the bigger boulders and can stay damp. The dozen problems cover a wide range, from the low V2 to V3 area through the mid V4 to V7 grades, with a few standout hard lines including a V10 highball and a V12 test piece. The forested surroundings give pine-needle ground in the neighbouring hollow, making this a good stop for stronger boulderers after a warm-up on the easier blocks nearby.

wa_a_west_alcove.blurb: A sport wall on the west end of Riverview Point in Echo Basin, part of the Frenchman Coulee climbing near Vantage. It sees little traffic because it sits a long way from the main parking lot, and it looks out over the Columbia River. Twelve sport routes run from 5.7 up to 5.11, with the greatest number around 5.10 and a few at 5.11, so it is one of the more reachable places in the Coulee to try that grade. Several lines carry good star ratings.

wa_static_point.blurb: A remote dome in the Skykomish Valley, about an hour and a half from Seattle, known for long slab climbing that suits comfortable leaders on moderate ground. Most of the twelve routes are trad and fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a pair of 5.10 sport lines. Pitches are long, protection is largely bolts with runouts between them, and the faces catch the sun, so they can get hot. A long uphill hike keeps crowds away, and the feel is closer to alpine climbing than to a roadside crag.

wa_comb_the.blurb: A cluster of four vertical buttresses of knobby rock near Darrington, numbered from the first to the fourth tooth going left to right. It is the first crag you pass on the drive in, yet it is rarely visited. Climbs mix alpine and trad styles, mostly at 5.10 with a few at 5.11 and one easier line. The approach is harder than at the neighbouring crag, with no maintained trail and some route-finding through steep forest, so expect a long day and bring gloves for the brush.
